title: The offering

segments.voice: Yesterday, the peace: a handshake, a hug or a bow, and the risen Jesus's greeting passed along the pews. Your line was peace be with you. Who did you greet like you meant it? Day one thousand three hundred forty-four.

A wicker basket on the end of a long wooden pole swings down the row, and a little girl drops in a coin she's been holding so tightly it's warm. Across town, a plate goes hand to hand, and someone slips in an envelope. In a third church, a family walks up the center aisle carrying a plate of bread and a small jug of wine, and hands them to the priest at the front. In a fourth, there's no basket at all, just a box by the door. Different churches, one moment in the service. Something is carried forward. Today: the offering.

Two kinds of gift come forward at the offering. There's money for the church and the poor. And in churches celebrating communion that day, there's the bread and wine for the table, sometimes carried up by people from the pews. In the Orthodox liturgy, the bread and wine are carried through the church in a slow procession called the Great Entrance. Here's the idea underneath both, and it comes from King David. In First Chronicles, the people have just given freely toward building the temple, gold and silver and more. And David doesn't congratulate them. He blesses God, and in the King James Bible he says this: "But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly after this sort? for all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee." It turns giving inside out. Nothing was theirs to begin with. They are handing back what they were handed. Some churches say that line as the gifts are brought forward. And the Orthodox liturgy, as the bread and wine are lifted up, says something close: thine own of thine own. Then the size of a gift. In Mark's Gospel, Jesus sits near the temple treasury watching people give. Rich people put in much. A poor widow puts in two small coins. Jesus calls his disciples over: "this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury." They gave from what they had left over. She gave all she had. And then the spirit of it. Paul writes, "God loveth a cheerful giver." Not grudgingly, he says, not because you have to.
screen: `OF THINE OWN HAVE WE GIVEN THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give something. Settle, and breathe. Turn your hands palm up on your knees, as if something has just been put in them. Let a few things you were given come to mind: this breath, a person who taught you, a skill, a meal you'll eat today. Then choose one small gift to pass on. Some money to a cause, an hour of your time, a call to someone lonely, a meal for a neighbor. Decide it now, so it's real. If you pray, you can say David's words: all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee. The bell holds the time.
The offering. The moment when gifts and bread are carried forward, handing back to God what Christians say was God's to begin with.

Your line: all things come of thee. This week went from the word preached and the gathered silence, through the spirit moving, one line to keep, the creed and the peace, to the offering. Today, give away the gift you chose, and give it cheerfully. Day one thousand three hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: In many churches an offering of money is collected during the service, by plate, basket or box, and where communion is celebrated the bread and wine are brought to the table at this point; in the Orthodox Divine Liturgy they are carried in procession in the Great Entrance.

original.note: Greek, from the Orthodox Divine Liturgy: thine own of thine own, said as the bread and wine are offered.

trapdoor: what you thought: the offering is when the church asks for money.
what it means: gifts and bread carried forward as worship, handing back what was given.
what a scholar hears: David's "of thine own have we given thee" turns giving inside out, and the Orthodox liturgy's "thine own of thine own" says the same.
